content: The investigational regimen for treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) includes a combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) administered over 24 weeks. In a Stage 2 trial, Arm 1 evaluated the addition of moxifloxacin to this regimen (BPaLM), while other arms included variations such as the addition of clofazimine (BPaLC). These regimens were compared to locally approved standard-of-care treatments, which were aligned as much as possible with World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for rifampin-resistant (RR) or MDR-TB. Patients were included in the comparative analyses if they were assigned to receive 24 weeks of therapy with BPaL, BPaLM, or BPaLC. The standard-of-care regimens used as comparators varied by country and included injectable-containing regimens lasting 9–11 months, all-oral regimens lasting 9–11 months, and longer regimens lasting 18–24 months. These regimens were consistent with WHO guidelines at the time of the trial. The primary outcome of the trial was the percentage of patients with unfavorable outcomes at 72 weeks post-randomization. Unfavorable outcomes included death, treatment failure, treatment discontinuation, loss to follow-up, ongoing treatment at 108 weeks, or recurrence of the disease. Clinical characteristics of the study population showed that the median age of participants was in the late 20s to early 30s, with a majority being male. HIV positivity was observed in approximately 27% of participants, and 43% had a history of prior TB treatment. The trial outcomes demonstrated that the BPaL-based regimens were associated with higher treatment success rates compared to standard-of-care regimens. For example, the success rate for BPaLM was 73%, compared to 58% for standard-of-care regimens. The BPaL regimens also showed lower rates of treatment failure, recurrence, and loss to follow-up. However, adverse events of Grade 3 or higher were reported in approximately 55% of participants across all regimens. The trial faced limitations, including small sample sizes, differences in baseline characteristics between groups, and variability in standard-of-care regimens across countries. Additionally, the trial was stopped early for benefit, which may introduce bias. Despite these challenges, the findings suggest that shorter BPaL-based regimens may offer improved outcomes for patients with MDR-TB, particularly in settings where standard-of-care regimens are less effective. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and address the limitations of the study.
